extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of American constitutional history / scholars of political institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and standards for creating and evaluating a national (federal) constitution and government, as discussed in a history/textbook chapter on the origin and nature of the U.S. Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential objects of the government
rubrics_metrics.description: The framers set four objects as essential to the Constitution's excellence: (1) its vigour and efficiency; (2) the independence of each of its departments; (3) its dependence on the people; (4) the security under it of the freedom of the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains how these objects were sought: a strong executive for vigour; separation of legislative, executive, and judicial powers and checks/balances for departmental independence and security of freedom; making authorities elective and elections frequent to secure dependence on the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere of national (federal) matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government should handle matters common to the whole nation, specifically: war and peace; treaties and foreign relations; army and navy; federal courts; commerce (foreign and interstate); currency; copyright and patents; the post-office and post roads; taxation for national purposes; and protection of citizens against unjust or discriminating State legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list defines the principal subjects upon which the national legislature may legislate and the national executive and judiciary may act; all other matters remain within State authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers and checks and balances
rubrics_metrics.description: The separation of legislative, executive, and judicial functions, with a system of checks and balances, is essential to freedom and to prevent any one department from becoming tyrannical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter cites Montesquieu and shows the framers’ repeated reliance on this dogma; it is presented as a foundational evaluative principle for constitutional design and operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: A strong executive to secure vigour and efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong executive (the President) was created to ensure the vigour and efficiency of the national government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The framers modeled the President on the State Governor and aspects of the British Crown, balancing energy in government with checks to avoid tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on the people through elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional design must ensure the government's dependence on the people, achieved by making authorities elective and by holding frequent elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent elections and elective offices are presented as mechanisms to bind government to popular control and legitimize authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security of individual freedom under a written constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution should secure the freedom of the individual, including placing certain rights under the protection of a written constitution (the Bill/Declaration of Rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes that several conventions recommended amendments addressing fears of encroachment on liberties; ten amendments (1791) were adopted immediately, forming a Bill of Rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance central authority with state autonomy (avoid over-consolidation)
rubrics_metrics.description: While creating a durable central power, the Constitution must respect centrifugal forces and leave a wide sphere of action to State governments so as not to imperil national unity or extinguish local institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly frames the Constitution as 'an instrument of compromises' obliged to leave certain points unsettled to accommodate diverse interests of separate commonwealths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root the constitution in historical practice and slow growth
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution that grows slowly and is rooted in past institutions and experience is more likely to endure; the American Constitution contains little that is absolutely new and much that is as old as Magna Charta.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter emphasizes the advantage of having precedents, experience of State constitutions, and established legal principles rather than relying on purely a priori theoretical design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer tested methods; avoid rash experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Those designing a constitution should prefer methods and devices tested by experience (e.g., British and State precedents) rather than bold, untried innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The framers started from systems they had worked under (colonial and State governments), following 'old paths' and adapting familiar institutions to national needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written/rigid constitution as instrument for defining powers and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A written or rigid constitution provides clear statutory provisions defining and limiting powers of government organs, enabling practical understanding of how a system operates under fixed rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast is drawn with the English 'constitution' of customs and flexible precedents; having a written document taught the framers what could safely be included and where to leave room for development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow elasticity for unpredictable emergencies and development
rubrics_metrics.description: While definite in principle, a constitution should contain elasticity in details to allow for unforeseeable emergencies and necessary development over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter praises the Constitution’s 'judicious mixture of definiteness in principle with elasticity in details' and notes that time and experience correct early mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal principle: acts beyond legal competence are void
rubrics_metrics.description: Design should embody the common-law principle that an act done by any official or law-making body beyond its legal competence is void; this helps create multiple supreme authorities each within its defined sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application of this principle made possible the creation of a National government leaving scope for State governments while dividing national powers among distinct persons and bodies so none could absorb the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution as complementary to State constitutions (not exhaustive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A national constitution does not attempt to create organs to discharge all functions of civilized government; it presupposes and complements State governments, which continue to handle most domestic matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises that the federal Constitution must be read along with State Constitutions to cover the whole field of civil government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of constitutional style and drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-drafted constitution should possess simplicity, brevity, and precision of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes the American Constitution's 'simplicity, brevity, and precision' and its literary qualities praised contemporaneously; style is presented as an evaluative attribute contributing to practical success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratification procedure and thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution's legitimacy depends on an effective ratification method: the draft was submitted to specially chosen state conventions and would come into effect when nine States had ratified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter explains why ratification by conventions (rather than a plebiscite) mattered for acceptance, and notes the political consequences of the nine-state threshold on how states reacted and joined the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision for amendments to address fears and defects
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution should include an amendment mechanism so that recommended changes (e.g., to guard liberties) can be adopted by a specified legislative and state-majority process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several conventions accompanied acceptance of the Constitution with recommendations for amendments; the prescribed method (two-thirds in Congress and three-fourths of the States) enabled adoption of the first ten amendments in 1791.
